title: Hydrosphere: Oceans
tagline: Ocean relief, salinity, temperature, currents and tides, and why the oceans matter

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ICSE Class IX Geography syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). The salinity, temperature and current figures quoted are standard oceanographic values and are given as averages, because they vary from place to place. No board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

learningOutcomes: State the proportion of the Earth's water that is found in the oceans and describe the relief of the ocean floor.
Explain what salinity is, state the average value and give the factors that change it.
Describe how the temperature of the ocean changes with depth and latitude.
Distinguish between warm and cold ocean currents, state what causes them and explain their effects.
Explain the cause of tides, and distinguish between spring tides and neap tides.

overview.intro: The hydrosphere is all the water on the surface of the Earth, and by far the greater part of it, about 97 per cent, lies in the oceans. The remaining fraction is locked up in ice and glaciers or held as fresh water in rivers, lakes and underground. The oceans are not a featureless sheet of water. Their floor has a relief of its own, with a shallow fringe around the continents, a steep slope beyond it, wide abyssal plains in the deep basins, ridges along the lines where new sea floor is created and trenches where it is destroyed. The water itself has a chemistry, a temperature and a movement. Its salt content averages about 35 parts per thousand, its temperature falls from the surface to the deep water, and it is set in motion by winds and by the differences in density between water masses, producing the currents that carry heat from the equator to the poles and make the climate of the coasts far more temperate than they would otherwise be.

facts.label: Water distribution
facts.value: About 97 per cent of the Earth's water is in the oceans, about 2 per cent is locked in ice and glaciers and about 1 per cent is fresh water

facts.label: Ocean floor relief
facts.value: Continental shelf, continental slope, abyssal plain, mid-ocean ridge and deep trenches

facts.label: Average salinity
facts.value: About 35 parts per thousand, highest in the Red Sea and lowest in the Baltic Sea

facts.label: Cause of tides
facts.value: Mainly the gravitational pull of the Moon, with a smaller effect from the Sun

learn.title: The relief of the ocean floor

blocks.text: The floor of the ocean is not flat. From the edge of a continent outwards it runs through a series of distinct forms. The continental shelf is the shallow, gently sloping apron that surrounds each continent and is covered by shallow water; it is the most productive part of the sea and the easiest place to fish. At the edge of the shelf the floor drops steeply down the continental slope. Beyond the base of the slope lies the abyssal plain, the flattest and largest region of the ocean floor. Rising from the deep basins are the mid-ocean ridges, which mark the lines where new sea floor is created, and in the deepest parts lie the trenches, which mark the lines where it is destroyed.

blocks.caption: Table: features of the ocean floor
rows: Gently sloping apron round the continents, covered by shallow sea
Steep slope at the outer edge of the shelf
Gentler slope of broken material at the foot of the continental slope
Flat, wide floor of the ocean basins
Submarine mountain chain along the lines of creation of new sea floor
Narrow, deep depression along the lines where sea floor is destroyed

items: The continental shelf makes up only about 8 per cent of the ocean floor but carries the greater part of the world's fishing.
The deepest known point, in the Mariana Trench of the Pacific, is nearly 11,000 m below the surface.
Mid-ocean ridges run for tens of thousands of kilometres and are joined into a single system through the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific oceans.
Submarine canyons and deep-sea fans on the abyssal plains are cut by turbidity currents, dense flows of sediment-laden water that rush down the continental slope.
Islands of the Pacific and of the Caribbean are mostly the summits of submarine volcanoes.

learn.title: Salinity and temperature of the ocean

blocks.text: Salinity is the total amount of dissolved salts in the ocean water, and it is expressed in parts per thousand. The average salinity of the open ocean is about 35 parts per thousand, but it varies, and the variation is governed by a simple balance. Salinity is raised by evaporation, which removes pure water and leaves the salt behind, and it is lowered by the addition of fresh water from rain, from rivers, from the melting of ice and from melting glaciers. It is also lowered where fresh water is trapped in the Arctic and Antarctic ice. The result is that the highest salinities occur in the hot, dry, enclosed seas, and the lowest in the cold, wet, enclosed seas.

blocks.caption: Table: salinity and temperature of ocean water
rows: Red Sea, about 40 parts per thousand; hot, dry and enclosed
Baltic Sea, about 7 parts per thousand; cold, wet and nearly enclosed
Highest at the Equator, about 27 to 30 degrees Celsius; falls towards the poles
Falls rapidly in the thermocline, then very slowly in the deep water
Fresh, because the salts are left behind as the ice forms

items: Salinity is raised by evaporation and lowered by rainfall, river inflow and the melting of ice and glaciers.
The upper layer of warm surface water is called the mixed layer, and it is stirred by wind and waves.
Below the mixed layer the temperature falls quickly with depth through the thermocline, reaching about 4 degrees Celsius in the deep water.
The deep water of the ocean is cold but it does not freeze, because pressure raises the freezing point and because the water is salty.
The warm layer of the tropical ocean extends deeper than the cold layer of the polar oceans, because the sun heats the tropics more strongly.

blocks.text: Ocean currents are the movement of seawater in a definite direction. The great currents are driven by the prevailing winds, and the trade winds drive warm currents in the tropics while the westerlies drive cold currents in the temperate latitudes. The rotation of the Earth deflects the moving water, so in the Northern Hemisphere currents turn to the right and in the Southern Hemisphere to the left, and this is what produces the great circulation systems and the gyres of the subtropical oceans. Continents get in the way and force the currents to turn. Warm currents flowing from the equator to the higher latitudes raise the temperature and the humidity of the coasts they pass, and cold currents flowing from the poles lower them.

items.meaning: A current that flows from the equator towards the poles and carries heat, warming the climate of the coast it passes.
A current that flows from the higher latitudes towards the equator and cools the climate of the coast it passes.
The great circular pattern of ocean currents in each of the subtropical oceans.
The regular rise and fall of the sea level, produced mainly by the gravitational pull of the Moon.
A tide of large range occurring at the new and full moon, when the Sun and the Moon pull in the same line.
A tide of small range occurring at the quarter moon, when the pulls of the Sun and the Moon are at right angles.

items: The Gulf Stream, the North Atlantic Drift and the Kuroshio are warm currents; the California, Peru, Benguela and Labrador currents are cold ones.
The warm North Atlantic Drift keeps the ports of north-west Europe free of ice in winter, at latitudes far to the north of those of eastern Canada.
The Peru current brings cold water to the west coast of South America and is one of the richest fishing grounds of the world, because of the upwelling of nutrient-rich deep water.
Tides are greatest at the new and full moon and smallest at the quarter moon, and the range of the tide is much greater in a funnel-shaped bay than on an open coast.
In the Indian Ocean the monsoon reverses the direction of the currents twice a year, a feature that is unique to that ocean.

blocks.text: The oceans make life on land possible. They store and transport enormous quantities of heat, and the great ocean currents carry that heat from the equator into the higher latitudes, so coastal places are far milder than the interiors of the continents at the same latitude. They supply the oxygen on which nearly all animal life depends, because the tiny floating plants of the ocean, the phytoplankton, produce a very large share of the oxygen of the atmosphere. They are the source of the world's main fishery, of petroleum and natural gas, of salt, and of the raw materials for many industries, and they carry more than half the world's freight and most of its communications cables.

items: The oceans moderate the climate of the world and soften the difference between day and night and between summer and winter.
Phytoplankton produce a large part of the oxygen of the atmosphere and are the base of the food chain of the sea.
The continental shelves hold most of the world's oil and natural gas, and the world's major fishing grounds.
Oceans provide food for billions of people and are a major source of protein.
Sea routes carry a large share of world trade, and submarine cables carry most of the internet traffic between the continents.
The oceans are a growing source of renewable energy through tidal power, wave power and ocean thermal difference.
They are also the final destination of much of the world's waste, and their pollution is one of the most serious problems of the present day.

figures.caption: Figure: Relief of the ocean floor
figures.description: From the shore the sea floor descends in a series of steps: the gently sloping continental shelf, the steep continental slope, the continental rise and then the flat abyssal plain, with mid-ocean ridges rising from it and deep trenches cutting into it.

figures.caption: Figure: Warm and cold currents in the Atlantic
figures.description: The trade winds drive the warm Gulf Stream northwards along the coast of North America, the North Atlantic Drift carries heat towards Europe, and the cold currents of the Labrador and Canary flow back towards the equator, completing the gyre.

keyPoints: About 97 per cent of the Earth's water is in the oceans, about 2 per cent is locked in ice and glaciers and about 1 per cent is fresh water.
The ocean floor has a continental shelf, a continental slope, a continental rise, abyssal plains, mid-ocean ridges and deep trenches.
The continental shelf is shallow, is the most productive part of the sea and carries most of the world's fishing.
Average ocean salinity is about 35 parts per thousand.
Salinity is raised by evaporation and lowered by rainfall, river inflow and the melting of ice.
The Red Sea has the highest salinity and the Baltic Sea the lowest.
Surface temperature is highest at the Equator and falls towards the poles; temperature falls rapidly through the thermocline.
Ocean currents are driven mainly by the prevailing winds and are deflected by the rotation of the Earth.
Warm currents warm the coasts they pass and cold currents cool them; the North Atlantic Drift keeps western Europe free of ice.
Tides are caused mainly by the gravitational pull of the Moon; spring tides are greatest at the new and full moon and neap tides smallest at the quarter moon.
Oceans moderate the world's climate, produce much of its oxygen, and provide food, minerals, transport and energy.
examFocus: Questions on the ocean floor usually ask for the order of the features from the shore outwards; learn that order as a sequence.
A salinity question must link the cause to the effect, for example 'evaporation raises salinity, so the Red Sea, which is hot, dry and enclosed, has the highest salinity'.
When asked why the North Atlantic Drift matters, explain the effect on the climate of the coasts, not the mechanism of the current alone.
Spring and neap tides are almost always set as a comparison; give the position of the moon and the relative strength of the two pulls.
For the importance of the oceans, give one point for the climate, one for the oxygen supply, one for food, one for minerals and one for transport, with a reason for each.

vocabulary.meaning: All the water on the surface of the Earth.
The shallow, gently sloping apron of sea floor around a continent.
The flat, deep floor of an ocean basin.
The total amount of dissolved salts in sea water, expressed in parts per thousand.
The layer of the ocean in which temperature falls rapidly with depth.
The continuous movement of seawater in a definite direction.
The great circular system of surface currents in a subtropical ocean.
The regular rise and fall of the sea level caused by the pull of the Moon and the Sun.

questions.prompt: The average salinity of the open ocean is about:
questions.explanation: The average salinity of the open ocean is about 35 parts per thousand. The Baltic Sea, at about 7, is the least saline and the Red Sea, at about 40, the most saline.
questions.commonMistake: Giving 40, which is the figure for the Red Sea and not the ocean average.

questions.prompt: The flat, wide floor of an ocean basin is called the:
questions.explanation: The abyssal plain is the flat floor of the deep ocean basin, lying at depths of about 3,000 to 6,000 m. The continental shelf is the shallow apron around the continents.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing continental shelf, which is shallow and near the shore rather than deep and flat.

questions.prompt: The tides are highest when the Sun and the Moon are:
options: At right angles to each other
At the same distance from the Earth
questions.explanation: At the new and full moon the pulls of the Sun and the Moon act in the same line, so their effects are added and the tide range is greatest. This is a spring tide.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing the quarter moon, which produces neap tides of small range because the two pulls are at right angles.

questions.prompt: A cold ocean current flowing along a coast lowers the temperature and the humidity of that coast. The current along the west coast of South America is the:
questions.explanation: The Peru, or Humboldt, current is a cold current that flows northwards along the west coast of South America and produces the cool, dry conditions of the coastal desert of Atacama. The Gulf Stream, the North Atlantic Drift and the Kuroshio are all warm currents.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing the Gulf Stream, which is a warm current on the other side of the Atlantic.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the greatest rise of the sea level caused by the joint pull of the Sun and the Moon at the new and full moon is called a ________ tide.
questions.explanation: A spring tide has the greatest range, occurring when the Sun and the Moon are in line with the Earth. A neap tide has the smallest range and occurs at the quarter moon.
questions.commonMistake: Answering 'neap tide', which is the tide of small range at the quarter moon.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the layer of the ocean in which temperature falls rapidly with depth is called the ________.
questions.explanation: Below the wind-stirred mixed layer the temperature falls steeply through the thermocline and then very slowly in the deep water, which stays near 4 degrees Celsius.
questions.commonMistake: Answering 'mixed layer', which is the surface layer that wind and waves stir and in which the temperature is nearly uniform.

questions.prompt: Explain why the Red Sea has a much higher salinity than the Baltic Sea.
questions.answer: Salinity depends on the balance between evaporation and the supply of fresh water. The Red Sea lies in a hot, dry region, so evaporation is intense and there is little rainfall and almost no river inflow to replace the water that is lost; being nearly enclosed, it also has no free exchange with the open ocean. The Baltic Sea lies in a cold region, so evaporation is weak, and it receives a large supply of fresh water from rain, from the rivers that drain into it and from the melting of ice and snow. Its salinity is therefore very low, at about 7 parts per thousand, compared with about 40 in the Red Sea.
questions.explanation: The explanation is a balance: the same factors of evaporation and fresh-water supply, working in opposite directions in the two seas.
questions.commonMistake: Mentioning only the climate and forgetting that the Red Sea is nearly enclosed and so loses no salt by exchange.

questions.prompt: Explain how ocean currents are formed and state the effect of a warm current on the climate of the coast it reaches.
questions.answer: Ocean currents are formed mainly by the friction of the prevailing winds on the surface of the sea, which drives the water in the direction of the wind, and by the difference in density between water masses of different temperature and salinity. The rotation of the Earth then deflects the moving water to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere, and the continents force the currents to turn, so that the great circulation systems and gyres are formed. A warm current carries heat from the lower latitudes towards the higher ones and raises the temperature and the humidity of the coast it reaches, which is why western Europe, reached by the warm North Atlantic Drift, is far milder than eastern Canada at the same latitude.
questions.explanation: A full answer gives the causes in order and then applies the effect of a warm current to a named example.
questions.commonMistake: Giving only the effect of the current without explaining how it is formed, which loses the first half of the question.

questions.prompt: Name three features of the ocean floor and give their depths.
questions.answer: The continental shelf runs from the shore to the edge of the land, to a depth of about 200 m, and slopes gently. The continental slope follows, dropping steeply from about 200 m to about 2,000 m. The continental rise lies at the foot of the slope between about 2,000 and 3,000 m. The abyssal plain, the flattest part of the ocean floor, lies between about 3,000 and 6,000 m, and the deepest trenches go down to about 11,000 m. Mid-ocean ridges rise above the abyssal plains as chains of submarine mountains.
questions.explanation: Naming the features with a depth for each is what the question requires, and the order from the shore outwards helps.
questions.commonMistake: Naming features of the coast such as a lagoon or a spit, which are not features of the ocean floor.

questions.prompt: Explain how the oceans influence the climate of the world and of the coastal areas, and describe the part played by the phytoplankton.
questions.answer: The oceans store an enormous amount of heat, because water has a much greater capacity for heat than land, and they both absorb the Sun's heat in the tropics and release it in the higher latitudes. The great ocean currents carry that heat from the equator towards the poles, and the western coasts of the continents in the temperate latitudes are warmed by warm currents such as the Gulf Stream and the North Atlantic Drift, while the western coasts of the continents in the tropics are cooled by cold currents such as the Peru and California currents. This is why western Europe has a mild, rainy climate while the coast of North America at the same latitude is cold, and why the coastal desert of Atacama exists on the west coast of South America. The oceans also moderate the temperature of the land, and the immense heat stored in them is released slowly, so that the coastal regions have smaller differences between day and night and between summer and winter than the interior of the continents. The phytoplankton are the microscopic floating plants of the ocean. They are the base of the food chain of the sea, because the fish feed on them directly or through the animals that feed on them, and through them the fisheries of the world are sustained. In addition they carry out photosynthesis in the enormous volume of sunlit surface water, and they are responsible for a very large share of the oxygen of the atmosphere, so they are one of the reasons for the survival of life on land.
questions.explanation: The answer has two clear strands, the transport and storage of heat, and the biological role of the phytoplankton, each tied to a named example.
questions.commonMistake: Saying only that the oceans moderate the climate, without the mechanism of the currents and without a named example.

questions.prompt: Examine the statement that the sea is the most important part of the Earth's environment.
questions.answer: The statement can be defended on strong grounds, although it needs to be qualified in a few places. The sea covers about 71 per cent of the Earth's surface and holds about 97 per cent of its water, so it is the largest single environment on the planet. It is the source of the oxygen on which nearly all animal life depends, because the phytoplankton of the sunlit surface waters carry out photosynthesis on a vast scale, and they are the base of the food chain that supports the fisheries on which billions of people depend. The sea stores and moves the heat that moderates the climate of the whole world, which is why the coasts and the maritime regions have mild climates while the interiors of the continents have extreme ones. It is the source of petroleum and natural gas, of salt, of fish and of the raw materials of many industries, it carries a large share of world trade and nearly all the submarine communication cables, and it is a fast-growing source of renewable energy from waves, tides and temperature differences. The qualification is that the sea is also the part of the environment that is worst affected by human activity, since the pollution of the sea, the depletion of the fisheries, the loss of the coral reefs and the rising temperature and acidity of the water are all serious problems of the present day, and because the sea is slow to recover, damage done to it is far less easily undone than damage to land.
questions.explanation: A good answer argues the case with named evidence, then shows the one serious qualification rather than simply agreeing.
questions.commonMistake: Agreeing without qualification, which gives no credit for the balanced part of the question.
